notes.definition: A mixture consists of two or more elements or compounds that are not chemically combined together. Mixtures can be separated by physical processes, which do not involve chemical reactions.
explanation: A mixture contains two or more elements or compounds that are not chemically combined. Because the substances are not bonded to each other, the chemical properties of each substance in the mixture are unchanged, and the proportions can vary. Air (mainly nitrogen and oxygen), sea water (salt dissolved in water), crude oil and ink are all mixtures. Mixtures can be separated by physical processes such as filtration, crystallisation, simple distillation, fractional distillation and chromatography. These processes do not involve chemical reactions, and no new substances are made.

Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. The mixture is poured through filter paper in a funnel. The liquid passes through the tiny holes in the paper and is called the filtrate. The solid particles are too big to pass through and stay on the paper; this is the residue. For example, filtering a mixture of sand and salt solution leaves sand as the residue and salt solution as the filtrate.

Crystallisation obtains a soluble solid from a solution. The solution is heated in an evaporating basin to evaporate some of the solvent until the solution is saturated (crystals start to form on a cold glass rod dipped into it). The solution is then left to cool, so crystals of the solid form as it becomes less soluble. The crystals are filtered off and dried, for example between filter papers or in a warm oven. Crystallisation gives purer, larger crystals than heating to dryness, which can make the solid spit or decompose.

Simple distillation separates a solvent from a solution, for example pure water from sea water or ink. The solution is heated so the solvent boils. The vapour leaves the flask and passes into a condenser, which is cooled by cold water flowing in at the bottom and out at the top. The vapour condenses back to a liquid, called the distillate, which is collected. The dissolved solid has a much higher boiling point, so it stays in the flask. Simple distillation works when the substances have very different boiling points.

Fractional distillation separates a mixture of liquids whose boiling points are close together, such as ethanol (78 °C) and water (100 °C), or the many hydrocarbons in crude oil. A fractionating column, packed with glass beads, is placed above the flask. The column is hottest at the bottom and coolest at the top. Vapours condense and re-evaporate many times as they rise, so the liquid with the lowest boiling point reaches the top first and passes into the condenser. When the thermometer reading rises, the next liquid is starting to distil, so the collecting container is changed.

Paper chromatography separates substances dissolved in a solvent, such as the different dyes in an ink. A spot of the mixture is placed on a pencil line on chromatography paper, and the bottom of the paper is dipped in a solvent. As the solvent moves up the paper it carries the dissolved substances with it, but different substances move at different rates, so they separate into different spots. To choose a separation method, think about the property the substances differ in: whether they are soluble or insoluble, whether you want the solid or the liquid, and how different their boiling points are.
keyFacts: A mixture contains two or more substances not chemically combined.
Each substance in a mixture keeps its own chemical properties.
Mixtures are separated by physical processes; no new substances are made.
Filtration: separates an insoluble solid (residue) from a liquid (filtrate).
Crystallisation: obtains a soluble solid from a solution by evaporating some solvent, then cooling.
Simple distillation: obtains a solvent from a solution, for example pure water from salt water.
Fractional distillation: separates liquids with similar boiling points, for example ethanol and water, or crude oil.
Chromatography: separates dissolved substances, such as dyes, that move at different rates through paper.
Condenser water enters at the bottom and leaves at the top, so the condenser stays full of cold water.
The lowest boiling point liquid distils first in fractional distillation.

keyTerms.definition: Two or more elements or compounds that are not chemically combined together.
The liquid (or solution) that passes through the filter paper during filtration.
The insoluble solid left on the filter paper after filtration.
Obtaining a soluble solid from a solution by evaporating some of the solvent and leaving the solution to cool so crystals form.
Separating a solvent from a solution by boiling the solvent and condensing the vapour.
Separating a mixture of liquids with similar boiling points using a fractionating column.
The liquid collected after the vapour is condensed in distillation.
A method of separating dissolved substances that move at different rates through a stationary material such as paper.
A change in which no new substances are made, such as dissolving, evaporating or condensing.

workedExamples.title: Choosing a separation method
workedExamples.question: Suggest how to obtain dry crystals of copper sulfate from a mixture of copper sulfate solution and insoluble copper oxide.
steps: Copper oxide is insoluble, so remove it first by filtration. It stays on the filter paper as the residue.
The filtrate is copper sulfate solution. Copper sulfate is soluble, so use crystallisation.
Heat the filtrate in an evaporating basin until crystals start to form, then leave it to cool.
Filter off the crystals and dry them between filter papers.
workedExamples.answer: Filter to remove copper oxide, then crystallise copper sulfate from the filtrate and dry the crystals.

workedExamples.title: Using boiling point data
workedExamples.question: Liquid A boils at 65 °C and liquid B boils at 82 °C. They mix completely. Which method separates them, and which liquid is collected first?
steps: The liquids mix, so filtration cannot separate them.
The boiling points are close together (17 °C apart), so simple distillation would not give a good separation; use fractional distillation.
The liquid with the lower boiling point reaches the top of the column first.
workedExamples.answer: Fractional distillation; liquid A (65 °C) is collected first.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that dissolving salt in water makes a new substance.
misconceptions.right: In fact salt solution is a mixture. The salt and water are not chemically combined and the salt can be recovered by crystallisation.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think filtration can remove dissolved salt from water.
misconceptions.right: In fact dissolved particles are small enough to pass through filter paper. Filtration only removes insoluble solids; distillation is needed to get pure water.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often say the filtrate is the solid left in the filter paper.
misconceptions.right: In fact the filtrate is the liquid that passes through; the solid left behind is the residue.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think simple distillation can separate any two liquids.
misconceptions.right: In fact simple distillation only works well when boiling points are very different. Liquids with similar boiling points need fractional distillation.

realWorld: Oil refineries separate crude oil into fractions such as petrol, kerosene and diesel by fractional distillation.
Desalination plants in dry countries distil sea water to produce drinking water.
Nitrogen and oxygen are obtained from liquefied air by fractional distillation.
Forensic scientists use chromatography to compare inks from documents and food scientists use it to check food colourings.
examTips: Match the method to the mixture: insoluble solid and liquid → filtration; soluble solid from solution → crystallisation; solvent from solution → simple distillation; liquids with similar boiling points → fractional distillation; dyes → chromatography.
When describing crystallisation, include all stages: heat to evaporate some solvent, leave to cool, filter off crystals, dry them.
Use the words residue and filtrate correctly, and say why filtration works (solid particles are too large to pass through the paper).
In separation questions with data tables, quote the relevant boiling points or solubility to justify your method.
summary: A mixture has two or more substances not chemically combined.
Each substance keeps its own chemical properties.
Mixtures are separated by physical processes, which make no new substances.
Filtration separates insoluble solids; crystallisation recovers soluble solids.
Simple distillation recovers a solvent; fractional distillation separates liquids with similar boiling points.
Chromatography separates dissolved substances such as dyes.

questions.question: Which of these best describes a mixture?
options: Two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions
A substance made of only one type of atom
Two or more substances that are not chemically combined
A substance that can only be separated by a chemical reaction
markScheme: 1 mark: two or more substances that are not chemically combined
questions.explanation: In a mixture the substances are not bonded together. Chemically combined in fixed proportions describes a compound, and one type of atom describes an element.

questions.question: Which of these is a mixture?
markScheme: 1 mark: air
questions.explanation: Air contains nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and other gases that are not chemically combined. Water, carbon dioxide and sodium chloride are compounds.

questions.question: Which method is best for separating sand from water?
markScheme: 1 mark: filtration
questions.explanation: Sand is an insoluble solid, so it is trapped by filter paper while the water passes through.

questions.question: Which method is used to obtain pure water from sea water?
markScheme: 1 mark: simple distillation
questions.explanation: Water is boiled off, condensed and collected, leaving the dissolved salts behind. Filtration cannot remove dissolved salt, and crystallisation would recover the salt, not the water.

questions.question: Which method separates the different coloured dyes in a sample of ink?
markScheme: 1 mark: chromatography
questions.explanation: Dissolved dyes move up chromatography paper at different rates, so they separate into different spots.

questions.question: During filtration, what name is given to the solid left on the filter paper?
markScheme: 1 mark: residue
questions.explanation: The residue is the solid left on the paper. The filtrate is the liquid that passes through, and the distillate is collected in distillation.

questions.question: Ethanol boils at 78 °C and water boils at 100 °C. Which method is best for separating a mixture of ethanol and water?
markScheme: 1 mark: fractional distillation
questions.explanation: The two liquids mix completely and have boiling points close together, so a fractionating column is needed for a good separation. Simple distillation would collect a mixture of both.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the condenser in distillation?
options: To heat the solution so that it boils
To cool the vapour so that it turns back into a liquid
To measure the boiling point of the liquid
markScheme: 1 mark: to cool the vapour so that it condenses into a liquid
questions.explanation: Cold water around the condenser cools the vapour so it condenses into the distillate. The thermometer, not the condenser, measures temperature.

questions.question: Which statement about separating mixtures is correct?
options: New substances are made during separation
A chemical reaction is needed to separate a mixture
No new substances are made during separation
Mixtures can only be separated by filtration
markScheme: 1 mark: no new substances are made during separation
questions.explanation: Separation methods for mixtures are physical processes, so no chemical reactions happen and no new substances form.

questions.question: In the fractional distillation of a mixture of ethanol (boiling point 78 °C) and water (boiling point 100 °C), which liquid is collected first, and why?
options: Water, because it has the higher boiling point
Ethanol, because it has the lower boiling point
Ethanol, because it is denser than water
Both at the same time, because they are mixed
markScheme: 1 mark: ethanol, because it has the lower boiling point
questions.explanation: The column is cooler at the top. Only the vapour of the substance with the lower boiling point reaches the top without condensing, so ethanol distils first.

questions.question: Which order of steps would give pure, dry salt from a mixture of salt and sand?
options: Add water and stir, filter, crystallise the filtrate, dry the crystals
Add water and stir, distil, filter the distillate
Heat the mixture strongly, filter, dry
markScheme: 1 mark: add water and stir, filter, crystallise the filtrate, dry the crystals
questions.explanation: Salt dissolves in water but sand does not. Filtering removes the sand, and crystallising the filtrate recovers the salt. Filtering before adding water would not separate anything.

questions.question: A student wants crystals of hydrated copper sulfate from copper sulfate solution. Why is crystallisation better than heating the solution until all the water has gone?
options: Heating to dryness can make the solid spit or decompose, and gives smaller, less pure crystals
Crystallisation is a chemical reaction that makes copper sulfate
Heating to dryness turns the copper sulfate into copper
Crystallisation removes the insoluble impurities from the solution
markScheme: 1 mark: heating to dryness can make the solid spit or decompose, giving smaller, less pure crystals
questions.explanation: Strong heating can drive off water that is part of the crystals and cause spitting. Slow cooling lets larger, purer crystals form. Crystallisation is a physical process, and insoluble impurities are removed by filtration, not crystallisation.

questions.question: State what is meant by a mixture.
markScheme: 1 mark: two or more elements or compounds
1 mark: not chemically combined (together)
questions.explanation: Both parts are needed. The phrase not chemically combined is what distinguishes a mixture from a compound.

questions.question:
A mixture of sand and salt solution is filtered.
(a) Name the residue.
(b) Name the filtrate.
markScheme: 1 mark: (a) sand
1 mark: (b) salt solution / salt water
questions.explanation: Sand is insoluble and is trapped by the paper. The dissolved salt passes through with the water.

questions.question:
Suggest the best method to separate each mixture:
(a) chalk powder and water
(b) the food colourings in a sweet coating
markScheme: 1 mark: (a) filtration
1 mark: (b) chromatography
questions.explanation: Chalk is insoluble, so filtration works. Food colourings are dissolved dyes, which are separated by chromatography.

questions.question: Iron filings mixed with sulfur powder are still attracted to a magnet. Explain why.
markScheme: 1 mark: the iron is not chemically combined with the sulfur, so it keeps its properties (including being magnetic)
questions.explanation: In a mixture each substance keeps its chemical and physical properties because no new substance has been made.

questions.question: Describe how to obtain crystals of sodium chloride from sodium chloride solution.
markScheme: 1 mark: heat the solution (in an evaporating basin) to evaporate some of the water / until crystals start to form
1 mark: leave to cool so crystals form
1 mark: filter off the crystals and dry them (between filter papers or in a warm place)
questions.explanation: This is crystallisation. Evaporating some water makes the solution saturated, and cooling makes the salt crystallise out.

questions.question: Explain how simple distillation separates water from a solution of ink.
acceptedAnswers: dye has a higher boiling point
markScheme: 1 mark: water has a much lower boiling point than the dyes, so the water boils / evaporates
1 mark: the water vapour is cooled and condenses (in the condenser) while the dyes stay in the flask
questions.explanation: Simple distillation relies on a big difference in boiling points. The water is collected as the distillate.

questions.question: Air can be cooled until it becomes a liquid. Name the method used to separate nitrogen and oxygen from liquid air.
markScheme: 1 mark: fractional distillation
questions.explanation: Nitrogen and oxygen are liquids with boiling points close together, so fractional distillation is used.

questions.question: Crude oil is a mixture of many hydrocarbons. Name the process used to separate crude oil and the property of the hydrocarbons that it depends on.
markScheme: 1 mark: fractional distillation
1 mark: the hydrocarbons have different boiling points
questions.explanation: Hydrocarbons with similar boiling points condense at the same level in the column and are collected together as a fraction.

questions.question: Give two differences between a mixture and a compound.
markScheme: Any two from:
1 mark: in a mixture the substances are not chemically combined; in a compound they are
1 mark: a mixture can have any proportions; a compound has fixed proportions
1 mark: a mixture can be separated by physical processes; a compound needs a chemical reaction
1 mark: substances in a mixture keep their properties; a compound has different properties from its elements
questions.explanation: Each difference should compare both: say what is true of the mixture and of the compound.

questions.question: Ethanol boils at 78 °C and water at 100 °C. Explain why simple distillation does not give pure ethanol from a mixture of ethanol and water.
markScheme: 1 mark: the boiling points are close together
1 mark: so a lot of water also evaporates and condenses with the ethanol (a fractionating column is needed)
questions.explanation: At 78 °C water already has a significant amount of evaporation, so the distillate is a mixture. A fractionating column lets the water vapour condense and run back while the ethanol vapour passes over.

questions.question: In distillation the thermometer bulb is placed level with the side arm leading to the condenser. Explain why.
acceptedAnswers: boiling point of the substance being collected
markScheme: 1 mark: it measures the temperature of the vapour entering the condenser
1 mark: this is the boiling point of the substance being collected, so it shows which substance is distilling (and when to change the collecting container)
questions.explanation: If the bulb were in the liquid it would measure the temperature of the boiling mixture, not of the vapour that is actually being collected.

questions.question: Explain why cooling water enters the condenser at the lower end and leaves at the upper end.
markScheme: 1 mark: the condenser jacket stays completely full of water (no air gap at the top)
1 mark: so cooling is more efficient and all the vapour condenses
questions.explanation: Water entering at the top would drain out at the bottom and leave part of the jacket empty, so cooling would be less effective.

questions.question:
Rock salt is a mixture of sodium chloride and insoluble sand and grit.
Describe how a student could obtain pure, dry sodium chloride crystals from rock salt. Explain why each step works.
markScheme: Indicative content: crush the rock salt (using a pestle and mortar) to increase surface area; add to water and stir / warm to dissolve the sodium chloride; sodium chloride is soluble but sand and grit are insoluble; filter the mixture; sand and grit stay on the filter paper as the residue because the particles are too large to pass through; the filtrate is sodium chloride solution; heat the filtrate in an evaporating basin to evaporate some water until crystals start to form; leave to cool so crystals form; filter off the crystals; dry between filter papers or in a warm oven.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a logical, complete method (dissolve, filter, crystallise, dry) with explanations linked to solubility and to each technique.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): the main steps in a sensible order with some explanation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two relevant steps, for example add water or filter, with little or no explanation.
questions.explanation: The method relies on the difference in solubility: dissolving separates salt from sand, filtration removes the insoluble solid, and crystallisation recovers the soluble salt.

questions.question:
A bottle contains a mixture of propanone (boiling point 56 °C) and water (boiling point 100 °C). A blue dye is dissolved in the mixture.
Describe and explain how a student could obtain separate samples of pure propanone and pure water, and how they could find out whether the blue dye is a single substance.
markScheme: Indicative content: propanone and water mix completely so filtration cannot be used; use fractional distillation because both are liquids; heat the mixture in a flask with a fractionating column; propanone has the lower boiling point so its vapour reaches the top first; collect the liquid that distils while the thermometer reads about 56 °C; when the temperature rises towards 100 °C change the collecting container; collect water at 100 °C; the dye has a much higher boiling point and stays in the flask; condenser cools the vapour with water in at the bottom; to test the dye use paper chromatography; spot the dye on a pencil line, place in solvent below the line; if it gives one spot it may be a single substance, more than one spot means it is a mixture of dyes.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): correct choice and detailed explanation of fractional distillation linked to boiling points, including the order of collection, and a correct use of chromatography to test the dye.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): identifies distillation and chromatography with some explanation, or a detailed explanation of only one technique.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): names one suitable technique or makes simple relevant points.
questions.explanation: Each technique matches a property: different boiling points for the two liquids, and different rates of movement on paper for dyes. Simple distillation is a weaker answer because 56 °C and 100 °C are close enough that the first distillate would contain some water.

questions.question: Compare simple distillation and fractional distillation. In your answer, give one example of a mixture separated by each method.
markScheme: Indicative content: both separate substances by boiling then condensing; both use a condenser and thermometer; simple distillation separates a solvent from a solution, or liquids with very different boiling points; example: water from salt water / sea water / ink; fractional distillation separates liquids with similar boiling points; it uses a fractionating column with a temperature gradient (hot at bottom, cool at top); the lowest boiling point liquid is collected first; example: ethanol and water / crude oil / liquid air.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear similarities and differences, including the fractionating column and boiling point difference, with a correct example for each.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct statements about one or both methods, or examples without explanation.
questions.explanation: A comparison needs points about both methods. The key difference is how close the boiling points are, which is why fractional distillation needs a column.
